title: The cost of mercy
hook: Dorothy Day lived the works of mercy at a personal cost

segments.voice: Yesterday, Caritas: the love God is, and the Church's work for the poor that carries its name. Your line was charity everywhere. Where did you spot it? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-four.

Soup on a stove in a New York kitchen. Coffee for whoever comes in off the street. Beds upstairs, not enough of them, and a woman who lives in the same house as the people she feeds, eats the same soup, and shares the same bathroom. Her name was Dorothy Day. With a friend, Peter Maurin, she started a newspaper called the Catholic Worker, and then houses of hospitality where people in need could simply stay. Yesterday was about charity that is organized and wide. Today is about what it costs the one who gives.
screen: `SOUP, COFFEE, NOT ENOUGH BEDS.` → `DOROTHY DAY.` → `HOUSES OF HOSPITALITY.`

segments.voice: First, her rulebook. Day kept pointing to Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus lists the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick and the prisoner, and says that whatever is done for them is done for him. "I was a stranger, and you took me in," in the Douay-Rheims. The Church gathers those deeds into the corporal works of mercy, and Day treated them less as good ideas and more as a daily schedule. Second, the cost. Living with the poor meant noise, smells, theft, people who were sick or angry or drunk, and very little privacy. It meant being tired most of the time. She went to jail for her protests. Mercy, in her house, was not something you dropped off on your way somewhere nicer. Third, why the cost doesn't cancel it. The story is told that Day didn't want to be called a saint, because a saint is easy to admire and easy to dismiss. If she was special, nobody else had to do it. She wanted the works of mercy to look ordinary, possible, within reach. Her cause for canonization has been opened anyway, and she is now called a Servant of God. Fourth, what the carry means. Some mercy costs nothing, and it's still good. But Day's life suggests that when mercy starts to cost you, sleep, comfort, money, the good opinion of others, that's often when it stops being a gesture and starts being love. Not suffering for its own sake. The cost is what makes it a gift. Some days, the cost is just an evening you had meant to keep for yourself.
screen: `HER RULEBOOK: MATTHEW 25.` · `NOISE, THEFT, NO PRIVACY.` · `A SAINT IS TOO EASY TO DISMISS.` · `THE COST MAKES IT A GIFT.` · then, large: `I WAS A STRANGER, AND YOU TOOK ME IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one costly kindness. Settle, and breathe. Let the list from Matthew walk slowly past: hungry, thirsty, stranger, naked, sick, prisoner. Notice which one tugs. Then ask what a kindness there would cost you this week. Not a grand plan. An hour. A visit you've been putting off. A meal for someone hard to be around. If there's reluctance, notice it honestly; it's part of the gift. If you pray, you can ask for the nerve to pay it. The bell holds the time.
The cost of mercy. Dorothy Day's lesson: the works of mercy, lived at a price, and the price is what turns a gesture into a gift. Today's word.
Your line: the cost is the point. Today, do one kindness that actually costs you something, time, comfort or pride, and pay it without keeping the receipt. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics practice the corporal works of mercy through soup kitchens, prison and hospital visits, and houses of hospitality like those of the Catholic Worker movement, which Dorothy Day co-founded.

original.note: Latin: mercy. the Latin Bible calls the merciful of Matthew 5:7 misericordes.

trapdoor: what you thought: mercy is being nice when it's easy.
what it means: the works of mercy, done even when they cost sleep, comfort or money.

notes: No dates given for Dorothy Day, the Catholic Worker or her cause. Confirm: co-founded with Peter Maurin; houses of hospitality; jailed more than once for protests; title Servant of God.
The 'don't call me a saint' line is widely attributed to her but is given here only as 'the story is told' and paraphrased; the screen head reads 'a saint is too easy to dismiss'.
The hook places her in a New York kitchen (the Catholic Worker began in New York). Confirm.
Original: Vulgate Matthew 5:7 'Beati misericordes'. No etymology of misericordia given. Confirm pronunciation (church Latin).

Editor pass: 'jail more than once' cut to 'jail for her protests' (no count under the claims rule); the practice no longer tells the listener they feel reluctance; 'ordinary Tuesday' stock line replaced; myth now says the works of mercy 'draw on' Matthew 25, since the Church's list also includes burying the dead.
The interpretation 'the cost is what makes it a gift' is the script's own reading of the carry, framed as what her life suggests.
